Spectral Decomposition of Euler-Mellin Integrals

Martin Helmer1\,{}^{1} and Felix Tellander2\,{}^{2} Email address: martin.helmer@swansea.ac.uk Email address: felix@tellander.se 1Department of Mathematics, Swansea University, Swansea, Wales, UK. 2Mathematical Institute, University of Oxford, Oxford OX2 6GG, UK
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We consider the spectral decomposition of singularities of integrals and their integrands. Our results apply to any integral of Euler-Mellin type, and thus especially to every scalar Feynman integral. Specifically we provide for both the integrand and integral respectively; two explicit constructions of the characteristic variety and characteristic cycle of the constructible function and DD-module they are associated with. From this we also obtain the singular locus or Landau singularities of the integral. En route we give a simple procedure to compute the local Euler obstruction function of a variety, and using this, to compute the Euler characteristic of the complex link of a Whitney stratum.

1. Introduction

Feynman integrals are a fundamental object underpinning a wide array of topics and calculations in modern physics [1]. As such there is significant interest in both understanding their mathematical structures and in computing them effectively. More broadly these integrals fall into the family of integrals of Euler-Mellin type, a generalization of the integrals studied in [2, 3]; that is integrals of the form

(1) ℐ⁡(z):=∫ℝ+nx1ν1⋯xnνnf1(x,z)λ1⋯fp(x,z)λp​d​x1x1∧⋯∧d​xnxn\mathcal{I}(z):=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}}\frac{x_{1}^{\nu_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{\nu_{n}}}{f_{1}(x,z)^{\lambda_{1}}\cdots f_{p}(x,z)^{\lambda_{p}}}\frac{dx_{1}}{x_{1}}\wedge\cdots\wedge\frac{dx_{n}}{x_{n}}

for any polynomials fi​(x,z)f_{i}(x,z) and fixed (but generic) constants λi\lambda_{i} and νj\nu_{j} where we treat xx as integration variables and zz as parameters.

In particular we seek to understand the singularities of the integral (1), that is the regions in ℂm∋z\mathbb{C}^{m}\ni z where the function (or distribution) ℐ⁡(z)\mathcal{I}(z) fails to be analytic. More precisely we seek to calculate the characteristic variety and cycle of the DD-module which annihilates ℐ⁡(z)\mathcal{I}(z) in a practical and effective manner.

In physics integrals of the form (1) with a single denominator polynomial f⁡(x,z)f(x,z) correspond to scalar Feynman integrals in the Lee-Pomeransky [4] representation. The singularities of these integrals are called Landau singularities [5] and studied in detail in e.g. [6, 7]. Knowing these singularities in advance may significantly aid the evaluation of the integrals, for example with the canonical differential equations approach [8]: They may constrain or even fully predict [9] the analytic building blocks or (symbol) letters [10] of this approach. This turns the derivation of the differential equations from a symbolic, to a much simpler numerical problem. Thanks to their utility, also in other aspects of Feynman integration [11], Landau analysis is currently experiencing a revival, see for example [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 9, 17, 18, 19, 20] and many others.

The physicist’s Landau singularity is directly related to the characteristic variety of the DD-module annihilating (1) by simply removing the zero-section and projecting onto the space of zz-variables. In this case, Theorem A below gives us the Landau singularities and Theorem C (see also Section 5) implies that the singular locus coincides with the so called Euler discriminant at codimension one, something that was recently proved in [21, Theorem 5.3].

In this note we will give two recipes which can be used to obtain this characteristic variety, and from it, the characteristic cycle. The first works by computing the blow-up of (a compactification of) the ambient space of the hypersurface defined by F=f1⋯fpF=f_{1}\cdots f_{p} along a Jacobian ideal derived from a certain hypersurface associated to FF. The second employs a coarsening of the Whitney stratification of the union of the (homogenization of the) hypersurface defined by FF with the coordinate hyperplanes xi=0x_{i}=0; the coarsening is obtained from certain multiplicity calculations for each strata.

We begin by considering the homogenization FhF_{h} of the product F=f1⋯fpF=f_{1}\cdots f_{p} in (1) as a polynomial in xx with respect to the new variable x0x_{0}; we then consider Fh​(x,z)F_{h}(x,z) as a polynomial in the ring ℂ⁡[x0,…,xn,z1,…,zm]\mathbb{C}[x_{0},\dots,x_{n},z_{1},\dots,z_{m}] and define G=x0⋯xnFhG=x_{0}\cdots x_{n}F_{h}.

From a computational perspective, perhaps surprisingly, using the recent algorithm of [22] to compute the Whitney stratification and the algorithm of [23] to compute multiplicities is often the most effective approach. The added benefit of this later approach is that we obtain C​C​(𝟙Y)CC(\mathbb{1}_{Y}), as well as the characteristic cycle of the DD-module associated to the annihilator ideal of GG.

To emphasize the practicality of our approach we have implemented these methods in the WhitneyStatifications Macaulay2 [24] package which may be downloaded at the link below:

http://martin-helmer.com/Software/WhitStrat/

The paper is arranged as follows. In Section 2 we introduce the necessary geometric constructions like Whitney stratifications, Euler obstructions and polar varieties. Following this in Section 3 we describe the annihilator ideal for one and several polynomials, their characteristic varieties, and how they relate to the microlocal description of the singularities of the solutions to these modules. In Section 4 we use the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence and Kashiwara’s index theorem to calculate the characteristic cycle of the DD-module annihilating the product of polynomials. This section also gives a method to compute the Euler characteristic of the complex link of a Whitney stratum (Remark 4.2). The integration of distributions and DD-modules are described in Section 5 where we also explicitly calculate the characteristic variety and cycle of several Euler-Mellin integrals.

We conclude this section with a simple example illustrating the main results. We note that in the example below we will present a Whitney stratification of a variety Y⊂ℂnY\subset\mathbb{C}^{n} in terms of closed sets to mirror the presentation used on a computer when computing such a stratification algorithmically.

2. Whitney Stratifications and Euler Obstructions

In this section we briefly review several important geometric constructions which will play a key role in our results in later sections.

Let ZZ be a variety of dimension dd. A Whitney stratification of ZZ is a subdivision into a finite number of smooth connected manifolds SαS_{\alpha}, called strata, such that Z=⋃αSαZ=\bigcup_{\alpha}{S_{\alpha}} and such that Whitney’s condition B holds for all pairs M=SαM=S_{\alpha}, N=SβN=S_{\beta}, of these manifolds. A pair of strata, M,NM,N, is said to be incident, denoted M⪯NM\preceq N if M⊆N¯M\subseteq\overline{N}. Incident strata M,NM,N satisfy Whitney’s condition B [25, Section 19] at a point x∈Mx\in M if for every sequence {pℓ}⊂M\{p_{\ell}\}\subset M and {qℓ}⊂N\{q_{\ell}\}\subset N with limpℓ=limqℓ=x\lim p_{\ell}=\lim q_{\ell}=x, the limit of secant lines between pℓ,qℓp_{\ell},q_{\ell} is contained in the limit of tangent planes to NN at qℓq_{\ell}. We say the pair M,NM,N satisfies condition B if condition B holds at all points x∈Mx\in M. For any M⊄N¯M\not\subset\overline{N} condition B is vacuously true. When computing Whitney stratifications, and representing them on a computer, it will often be convenient (as in e.g. [26, 22]) to represent the Whitney stratification as a flag Z∙Z_{\bullet} of varieties Z0⊂⋯⊂Zd=ZZ_{0}\subset\cdots\subset Z_{d}=Z where the strata are then the connected components of the successive differences Zi−Zi−1Z_{i}-Z_{i-1}.

Given a variety X=𝐕⁡(f1,…,fm)⊂ℂnX=\mathbf{V}(f_{1},\dots,f_{m})\subset\mathbb{C}^{n}, dim(X)=d\dim(X)=d, with fi∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], we let XSingX_{\rm Sing} denote the singular locus of XX and let Xreg=X−XSingX_{\rm reg}=X-X_{\rm Sing} denote the (open) manifold of smooth points in XX. The conormal variety of a variety X⊂ℂnX\subset\mathbb{C}^{n} is the subvariety of X×ℙn−1X\times\mathbb{P}^{n-1} given by

(4) 𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(X)={(p,ξ)|p∈Xreg​ and ​Tp​Xreg⊂ξ⟂}¯;\displaystyle{\rm\bf Con}(X)=\overline{\left\{(p,\xi)\;|\;p\in X_{\rm reg}\text{ and }T_{p}X_{\rm reg}\subset\xi^{\perp}\right\}};

as noted in the introduction 𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(X){\rm\bf Con}(X) can also be thought of as the Zariski closure of the conormal bundle to the smooth part of a variety (where we hence consider the direction vectors as projective to get a unique representative, up to projective equivalence, for each direction). We note that we can compute equations for 𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(X)\mathbf{Con}(X) in a straightforward manner. Work in the ring ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn,ξ1,…,ξn]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n},\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{n}] and set

𝔎=(ξ1⋯ξn∂f1∂x1⋯∂f1∂xn⋱∂fm∂x1⋯∂fm∂xn) and 𝔍=(∂f1∂x1⋯∂f1∂xn⋱∂fm∂x1⋯∂fm∂xn).\mathfrak{K}=\begin{pmatrix}\xi_{1}&\cdots&\xi_{n}\\ \frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}&\cdots&\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial x_{n}}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \frac{\partial f_{m}}{\partial x_{1}}&\cdots&\frac{\partial f_{m}}{\partial x_{n}}\\ \end{pmatrix}\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathfrak{J}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}&\cdots&\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial x_{n}}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \frac{\partial f_{m}}{\partial x_{1}}&\cdots&\frac{\partial f_{m}}{\partial x_{n}}\\ \end{pmatrix}.

Let KK be the ideal generated by all (n−d+1)×(n−d+1)(n-d+1)\times(n-d+1) minors of the matrix 𝔎\mathfrak{K}, and let JJ be the ideal defined by the (n−d)×(n−d)(n-d)\times(n-d) minors of the matrix 𝔍\mathfrak{J}. The conormal variety 𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(X)=𝐕⁡(I𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(X)){\rm\bf Con}(X)=\mathbf{V}(I_{{\rm\bf Con}(X)}) is defined by the radical ideal given by the saturation I𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(X)=(IX+K):J∞I_{{\rm\bf Con}(X)}=(I_{X}+K):J^{\infty}. Note also that XSing=𝐕⁡(J)X_{\rm Sing}=\mathbf{V}(J). Conormal varieties are naturally connected to Whitney stratification, see e.g. [26], where an algorithm to compute Whitney a stratification using conormal varieties is given.

A related concept is that of the polar varieties of XX; these are defined as follows. Consider a flag L∙L_{\bullet} of length dd

Pi​(X,L∙):={p∈Xreg∣dim(Tp​Xreg∩Li+1)>d−n+i+1}¯.P_{i}(X;L_{\bullet}):=\overline{{\left\{{p\in X_{\text{reg}}\mid\dim(T_{p}X_{\text{reg}}\cap L_{i+1})>d-n+i+1}\right\}}}.

where the cj(i)∈ℂc^{(i)}_{j}\in\mathbb{C} are general constants for i∈{0,…,d−1}i\in{\left\{{0,\dots,d-1}\right\}}. Let KiK_{i} be the ideal generated by all (n−d+i+1)×(n−d+i+1)(n-d+i+1)\times(n-d+i+1) minors of the matrix 𝔎i\mathfrak{K}_{i}. Then

where Li+1L_{i+1} is the linear space spanned by the first i+1i+1 rows of 𝔎i\mathfrak{K}_{i}.

Polar varieties contains a lot of geometric information. For example, they can be used to effectively calculate Whitney stratifications [22] and reduce them to a canonical coarsest stratification. Also note that the similarity in the equations of the polar and conormal varieties is not co-incidental, and in fact if we take πX:𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(X)→X\pi_{X}:\mathbf{Con}(X)\to X to be the natural projection, the polar variety Pi​(X,L∙)P_{i}(X;L_{\bullet}) is the image of the (closure of the) intersection of 𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(X)∩Li+1\mathbf{Con}(X)\cap L_{i+1} under the projection πX\pi_{X} where we treat Li+1L_{i+1} as an ii dimensional projective liner space.

Let Z⊂ℂnZ\subset\mathbb{C}^{n} be a complex variety, defined by the ideal IZI_{Z} and let W⊂ZW\subset Z be an irreducible variety defined by a prime ideal IWI_{W}. Recall that the multiplicity of ZZ along WW, denoted multW​(Z){\rm mult}_{W}(Z), is defined as the Hilbert-Samuel multiplicity (see e.g.[27, Chapter 12]) of the local ring (ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]/IZ)IW(\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]/I_{Z})_{I_{W}} at the prime ideal IWI_{W}; note that if pp is a general point in WW then multW​(Z)=multp​(Z){\rm mult}_{W}(Z)={\rm mult}_{p}(Z). If W∩Z=∅W\cap Z=\emptyset we define multW​(Z):=0{\rm mult}_{W}(Z):=0. These multiplicities can be computed efficiently using Segre classes [23].

In [28, Chapter V, Theorem 1.2] Teissier shows that two open strata M,NM,\,N with M⊂N¯M\subset\overline{N} satisfy Whitney’s condition B if and only if the sequence of Hilbert-Samuel multiplicities

mult∙​(N¯,z)={multz​P0​(N¯,L∙),…,multz​Pd−1​(N¯,L∙),multz​N¯}\mathrm{mult}_{\bullet}(\overline{N},z)=\{\mathrm{mult}_{z}P_{0}(\overline{N};L_{\bullet}),\ldots,\mathrm{mult}_{z}P_{d-1}(\overline{N};L_{\bullet}),\,\mathrm{mult}_{z}\overline{N}\}

is constant for every z∈Mz\in M. Given any Whitney stratification, strata with the same sequence of polar multiplicities can be joined to obtain a unique canonical coarsest Whitney stratification.

Another geometric construction that can be obtained from the polar varieties is the local Euler obstruction. The local Euler obstruction (or Euler obstruction) was introduced by MacPherson in his generalization of the Chern class to singular varieties [29], an object we now call the Chern-Schwartz-MacPherson (CSM) class. In this context, for a variety YY, it is thought of as a constructible function Y→ℤY\to\mathbb{Z} and is shown to take a constant value on each Whitney stata of YY.

The same invariant was also introduced by Kashiwara a year or so earlier [30] and we will use his recursive definition of this invariant. Let YY be a variety of dimension dd, fix a Whitney stratification Y=∪SαY=\cup S_{\alpha}, with dα=dim(Sα)d_{\alpha}=\dim(S_{\alpha}), and denote the Euler obstruction of S¯γ\overline{S}_{\gamma} along SαS_{\alpha} as 𝐄𝐮S¯γ​(Sα)\mathbf{Eu}_{\overline{S}_{\gamma}}(S_{\alpha}); as noted above the Euler obstruction takes a constant value on strata hence 𝐄𝐮S¯γ​(x)=𝐄𝐮S¯γ​(Sα)\mathbf{Eu}_{\overline{S}_{\gamma}}(x)=\mathbf{Eu}_{\overline{S}_{\gamma}}(S_{\alpha}) for all x∈Sαx\in S_{\alpha}. 3. Microlocal Analysis of DD-modules and Annihilator Ideals

The Weyl algebra DD on ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} is given by

(13) D:=R⟨∂1,…,∂n⟩,R=ℂ[x1,…,xn]D:=R\left<\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}\right>,\quad R=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]

where [xi,xj]=[∂i,∂j]=0[x_{i},\,x_{j}]=[\partial_{i},\,\partial_{j}]=0 and ∂ixj=xj∂i+δi​j\partial_{i}x_{j}=x_{j}\partial_{i}+\delta_{ij} for all 1≤i,j≤n1\leq i,j\leq n. To replace ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} with a general manifold XX, the ring RR is replaced by the sheaf of regular functions 𝒪X\mathscr{O}_{X} and DD is replaced by 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}, the sheaf of ℂ\mathbb{C}-linear differential operators on 𝒪X\mathscr{O}_{X}. A system of partial differential equations P1​u=0,…,Pk​u=0P_{1}u=0,\ldots,P_{k}u=0 is encoded as the left-ideal I=⟨P1,…,Pk⟩I=\left<P_{1},\ldots,P_{k}\right> and generates the DD-module M=D/I.M=D/I.

For a non-zero element pp in the Weyl algebra we define the principal symbol as the following initial form (cf. [36, Chapter 1]):

(14) σ​(p):=in(0,1)​(p).\sigma(p):=\mathrm{in}_{(0,1)}(p).

This is an element in the associated graded ring gr(0,1)​(D)=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn,ξ1,…,ξn]\mathrm{gr}_{(0,1)}(D)=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n}] which is a commutative ring in 2​n2n variables. For any left-ideal II in a Weyl algebra we can similarly define the characteristic ideal as the ideal containing all principal symbols of p∈Ip\in I:

(15) in(0,1)​(I):={σ⁡(p)|p∈I}.\mathrm{in}_{(0,1)}(I):=\{\sigma(p)\,|\,p\in I\}.

The characteristic variety describes regions where the solutions to the system of PDEs (partial differential equations) associated to II may be singular and is simply the variety defined by the characteristic ideal above, i.e.

Char⁡(I):=𝐕⁡(in(0,1)​(I)).\mathrm{Char}(I):=\mathbf{V}(\mathrm{in}_{(0,1)}(I)).

The characteristic ideal can directly be calculated using non-commutative Gröbner bases in e.g. Macaulay2 [24] and it is a theorem of Ōaku [37] that this definition coincides with the analytic DD-module definition using good filtrations for sheaves of modules. A DD-ideal (or module) is said to be holonomic if dim(Char⁡(I))=n\dim(\mathrm{Char}(I))=n. All DD-modules of interest in this paper are of an even nicer type called regular holonomic, however, we do not give the technical definition here, see e.g. [36, Definition 2.4.1] or [38, Definition 5.2] for two different but equivalent definitions.

Let {Λα}\{\Lambda_{\alpha}\} denote the irreducible components of Char⁡(I)\mathrm{Char}(I), or the irreducible components of the characteristic variety of any DD-module ℳ\mathscr{M}. We the construct the algebraic cycle

(16) C​C​(ℳ)=∑αmα​ΛαCC(\mathscr{M})=\sum_{\alpha}m_{\alpha}\Lambda_{\alpha}

called the characteristic cycle where the multiplicities mαm_{\alpha} are unique positive integers. For an intrinsic DD-module definition of mαm_{\alpha} see [39, Proposition 1.8.2]. For holonomic modules C​C​(ℳ)CC(\mathscr{M}) is a Lagrangian cycle. For a variety YY one may also define the characteristic cycle of the constructable function 𝟙Y\mathbb{1}_{Y}, in this case the multiplicities mαm_{\alpha} above are given by (10); see Section 4 for further discussion.

3.1. Characteristic Varieties and Spectral Properties of Distributions

The spectral decomposition of a distribution u∈𝒟′​(ℝn)u\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) gives complete microlocal information on its singularity structure. This decomposition is called the wave front set and describes not only where a distribution is singular but which components in the cotangent space are causing this behavior. We call a set Λ⊂ℝn×ℝn∖0\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus 0 conic if (x,ξ)∈Λ⟹(x,λ​ξ)∈Λ(x,\xi)\in\Lambda\implies(x,\lambda\xi)\in\Lambda for all real λ≠0\lambda\neq 0. This means that we could think of Λ\Lambda as being in ℝn×ℝ​ℙn−1\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}\mathbb{P}^{n-1}. For the construction of the analytic wave front set we follow the presentation by Treves [40, Section 3.5].

Definition 3.1.

Let vv be a distribution with compact support in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. We say that vv is microanalytic at a point (x′,ξ′)∈ℝn×ℝn∖0(x^{\prime},\xi^{\prime})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus 0 if there is a conic neighborhood Λ∋(x′,ξ′)\Lambda\ni(x^{\prime},\xi^{\prime}) and positive real numbers κ,c\kappa,\,c such that

(17) |∫ℝnei​ξ⋅(x−y)−κ​|ξ|​|x−y|2​ν​(y)​Δκ​(x−y,ξ)​𝑑y|≲e−c​|ξ|\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}e^{i\xi\cdot(x-y)-\kappa|\xi||x-y|^{2}}\nu(y)\Delta_{\kappa}(x-y,\xi)\,dy\right|\lesssim e^{-c|\xi|}

where Δκ​(x,ξ):=1+i​κ​(x⋅ξ)/|ξ|\Delta_{\kappa}(x,\xi):=1+i\kappa(x\cdot\xi)/|\xi| holds for all (x,ξ)∈Λ(x,\xi)\in\Lambda with |ξ||\xi| sufficiently large.

For a distribution u∈𝒟′​(Ω)u\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\Omega), with not necessarily compact support, we say that it is microanalytic at a point (x′,ξ′)∈Ω×ℝn∖0(x^{\prime},\xi^{\prime})\in\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus 0 if there is a distribution vv with compact support in Ω\Omega equal to uu in some neighborhood of x′x^{\prime} and microanalytic at (x′,ξ′)(x^{\prime},\xi^{\prime}).

Definition 3.2.

For a distribution u∈𝒟′​(Ω)u\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\Omega) we define the analytic wave front set W​FA​(u)WF_{A}(u) as the closed subset of Ω×ℝn∖0\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus 0 consisting of points (x′,ξ′)(x^{\prime},\xi^{\prime}) at which uu is not microanalytic.

The image of W​FA​(u)WF_{A}(u) under the canonical projection π:Ω×ℝn∖0→Ω:(x,ξ)↦x\pi:\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus 0\to\Omega:(x,\xi)\mapsto x is precisely the set where uu fails to be an analytic function.

We will now see that the analytic wave front set of a distribution is closely related to the characteristic variety of the differential operators that annihilate it. Let PP be a differential operator of order mm with analytic coefficients defined in an open set Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. It has the form

P=P(x,∂)=∑|α|≤maα(x)∂α.P=P(x,\partial)=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq m}a_{\alpha}(x)\partial^{\alpha}.

The principal symbol of PP, denoted σm\sigma_{m} is defined by

(18) σm​(x,ξ)=∑|α|=maα​(x)​ξα.\sigma_{m}(x,\xi)=\sum_{|\alpha|=m}a_{\alpha}(x)\xi^{\alpha}.

For polynomial coefficients this coincides with (14). The following result is by Hörmander [41, Theorem 8.6.1].

Theorem 3.3.

If PP is a differential operator of order mm with analytic coefficients, then

(19) W​FA​(u)⊂Char∗​(P)∪W​FA​(P​u),u∈𝒟′​(Ω),WF_{A}(u)\subset\mathrm{Char}^{*}(P)\cup WF_{A}(Pu),\quad u\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\Omega),

where Char∗​(P)={(x,ξ)∈T∗​Ω∖0|σm​(x,ξ)=0}\mathrm{Char}^{*}(P)=\{(x,\,\xi)\in T^{*}\Omega\setminus 0\,|\,\sigma_{m}(x,\xi)=0\}.

In particular if PP annihilates uu, i.e. P​u=0Pu=0, we have W​FA​(u)⊂Char∗​(P)WF_{A}(u)\subset\mathrm{Char}^{*}(P). This directly generalizes to the following result.

Corollary 3.4.

Let ℳ\mathscr{M} be the 𝒟Ω\mathscr{D}_{\Omega}-module consisting of all elements annihilating uu, then W​FA​(u)⊂Char⁡(ℳ)∖0∩(ℝn×ℝn∖0)WF_{A}(u)\subset\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M})\setminus 0\cap(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus 0).

3.2. Annihilator Ideals

Extending the coefficient field of the Weyl algebra from ℂ\mathbb{C} to polynomials ℂ⁡[s]\mathbb{C}[s] in a new commuting variable ss, we get the algebra D⁡[s]:=D⊗ℂℂ⁡[s]D[s]:=D\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}[s]. Denote by AnnD⁡[s]​(fs)\mathrm{Ann}_{D[s]}(f^{s}) the left-ideal

(20) AnnD⁡[s]​(fs):={Q∈D⁡[s]|Q∙fs=0}\mathrm{Ann}_{D[s]}(f^{s}):=\{Q\in D[s]\,|\,Q\bullet f^{s}=0\}

for any s∈ℂs\in\mathbb{C} and any xx with f⁡(x)≠0f(x)\neq 0, this is the parametric annihilator. It is a result by Bernstein [42] that for a non-zero polynomial f⁡(x)f(x) there exists a non-zero polynomial b⁡(s)b(s) and differential operator P⁡(s)∈D⁡[s]P(s)\in D[s] such that

(21) b⁡(s)​f​(x)s=P⁡(s)∙f​(x)s+1.b(s)f(x)^{s}=P(s)\bullet f(x)^{s+1}.

When b⁡(s)b(s) is chosen to be the monic polynomial of lowest possible degree, it is called the Bernstein-Sato polynomial.

The actual problem we are interested in is finding the annihilators of fλf^{\lambda} with λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C} being treated as a fixed number. Replacing s→λs\to\lambda in AnnD⁡[s]​(fs)\mathrm{Ann}_{D[s]}(f^{s}) give elements that annihilates fλf^{\lambda}, however, these elements might not fully generate AnnD​(fλ)\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(f^{\lambda}). The following theorem fully classifies when direct replacement provides the correct answer.

Theorem 3.5 ([36, Theorem 5.3.13]).

Let α0\alpha_{0} be the smallest integer root of the Bernstein-Sato polynomial of ff. If λ≠α0+k,k=1, 2,…\lambda\neq\alpha_{0}+k,\ k=1,\,2,\,\ldots, then AnnD​(fλ)\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(f^{\lambda}) is given by direct replacement s→λs\to\lambda in AnnD⁡[s]​(fs)\mathrm{Ann}_{D[s]}(f^{s}).

The annihilator ideal of fλf^{\lambda} for the λ\lambda not covered by the theorem can still be calculated by adding to the calculation of AnnD⁡[s]​(fs)\mathrm{Ann}_{D[s]}(f^{s}) the computation of a specific syzygy module. It turns out that the characteristic variety of annihilator ideals is always very well-behaved, see [36, Theorem 5.3.1] (c.f. [43]).

Theorem 3.6.

The ideal AnnD​(fλ)\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(f^{\lambda}) is regular holonomic for any λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C}.

Remark 3.7.

Throughout this work we will assume λ1,…,λp,ν1,…,νn\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{p},\nu_{1},\ldots,\nu_{n} in the integral (1) to be generic. ♠\spadesuit

Example 3.8.

Let f=x2​z−y2f=x^{2}z-y^{2} be the polynomial defining the Whitney umbrella Y=𝐕⁡(f)Y=\mathbf{V}(f). The parametric annihilator of this polynomial is the following left-ideal generated by six terms

AnnD⁡[s](fs)=⟨x∂x−2z∂z,y∂y+2z∂z−2s,xz∂y+y∂x,x2∂y+2y∂z, 2z2∂y∂z+y∂x2+z∂y⟩.\mathrm{Ann}_{D[s]}(f^{s})=\langle x\partial_{x}-2z\partial_{z},\,y\partial_{y}+2z\partial_{z}-2s,\,xz\partial_{y}+y\partial_{x},\,x^{2}\partial_{y}+2y\partial_{z},\,2z^{2}\partial_{y}\partial_{z}+y\partial_{x}^{2}+z\partial_{y}\rangle.

and the Bernstein-Sato polynomial is given by b⁡(s)=(s+1)2​(s+3/2)b(s)=(s+1)^{2}(s+3/2). By a simple Gröbner basis calculation we find the characteristic variety:

Char⁡(AnnD​(fλ))=\displaystyle\mathrm{Char}(\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(f^{\lambda}))= 𝐕⁡(y​η+2​z​ζ,x​ξ−2​z​ζ,x​z​η+y​ξ,x2​η+2​y​ζ)\displaystyle\mathbf{V}(y\eta+2z\zeta,x\xi-2z\zeta,xz\eta+y\xi,x^{2}\eta+2y\zeta)
=\displaystyle= 𝐕⁡(y​η+2​z​ζ,x​ξ−2​z​ζ,z​η2−ξ2,x​η2−2​ξ​ζ,x​z​η+y​ξ,x2​η+2​y​ζ,x2​z−y2)∪\displaystyle\mathbf{V}(y\eta+2z\zeta,x\xi-2z\zeta,z\eta^{2}-\xi^{2},x\eta^{2}-2\xi\zeta,xz\eta+y\xi,x^{2}\eta+2y\zeta,x^{2}z-y^{2})\cup
𝐕⁡(ζ,y,x)∪𝐕⁡(z,y,x)∪𝐕⁡(ζ,η,ξ)\displaystyle\mathbf{V}(\zeta,y,x)\cup\mathbf{V}(z,y,x)\cup\mathbf{V}(\zeta,\eta,\xi)
=\displaystyle= 𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(x2​z−y2)∪𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(x,y)∪𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(x,y,z)∪𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(0).\displaystyle\mathbf{Con}(x^{2}z-y^{2})\cup\mathbf{Con}(x,y)\cup\mathbf{Con}(x,y,z)\cup\mathbf{Con}(0).

The three components except the zero-section 𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(0)\mathbf{Con}(0) are shown in Figure 1. By calculating the multiplicity of the characteristic ideal along the irreducible components in the characteristic variety we get the characteristic cycle:

C​C​(AnnD​(fλ))=𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(x2​z−y2)+𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(x,y)+𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(x,y,z)+𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(0).CC(\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(f^{\lambda}))=\mathbf{Con}(x^{2}z-y^{2})+\mathbf{Con}(x,y)+\mathbf{Con}(x,y,z)+\mathbf{Con}(0).

3.3. The Characteristic Variety of An Annihilator Module of One Element

It is only very special DD-modules where the structure of the characteristic variety is known. If a DD-module is invariant under a group action, the geometry of the different group orbits dictate the characteristic variety [44, Theorem 5.1.12]. An example of this appears in the theory of generalized hypergeometry by Gelfand, Kapranov and Zelevinsky (GKZ) where the group is the algebraic torus and the characteristic variety is the union of conormal bundles of the AA-discriminants [45] associated to each face of the polytope of the AA-matrix defining the system [46, Theorem 4]. The example from the Introduction fits within this framework which we will revisit in Example 5.11, see also Example 5.10. We will see in this section that annihilator modules are another example where both the characteristic variety and cycle can be calculated explicitly.

3.3.1. Kashiwara’s Wf0W_{f}^{0} version of Characteristic Variety

We begin by recalling an explicit construction of the characteristic variety of AnnD​(fλ)\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(f^{\lambda}).

Definition 3.9.

Let ff be a holomorphic function on a smooth complex manifold XX11 1 For our purposes usually X=ℂnX=\mathbb{C}^{n}..

  • (i)

    Wfs{W}_{f}^{s} is the Zariski closure of the set

    {(s;x,ξ)∈ℂ×T∗X|x∈X,f(x)≠0,ξ=sdlogf(x)}inℂ×T∗X.\{(s;\,x,\,\xi)\in\mathbb{C}\times T^{*}X\,|\,x\in X,\ f(x)\neq 0,\ \xi=sd\log f(x)\}\quad\mathrm{in}\quad\mathbb{C}\times T^{*}X.

    Or in other words

    Wfs:={(s;x,ξ)∈ℂ×T∗X|x∈X,f(x)≠0,ξ=s​f′​(x)f⁡(x)}¯inℂ×T∗​X.{W}_{f}^{s}:=\overline{\left\{(s;\,x,\,\xi)\in\mathbb{C}\times T^{*}X\,|\,x\in X,\ f(x)\neq 0,\ \xi=\frac{sf^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}\right\}}\quad\mathrm{in}\quad\mathbb{C}\times T^{*}X.
  • (ii)

    Wf0:={(x,ξ)∈T∗​X|(0,x,ξ)∈Wfs}W_{f}^{0}:=\{(x,\,\xi)\in T^{*}X\,|\,(0;\,x,\,\xi)\in{W}_{f}^{s}\}

It is a classical result that Wf0W_{f}^{0}, called the relative conormal variety, is a Lagrangian variety. Examining the definition of Wf0W_{f}^{0} we see that it can be described as the vanishing set of the following ideal:

(22) 𝐈⁡(Wf0)=(⟨ξ1​f−σ⁡(∂1f),…,ξn​f−σ⁡(∂nf)⟩:⟨f⟩∞+⟨σ⟩)∩ℚ⁡[x1,…,xn,ξ1,…,ξn].\mathbf{I}(W_{f}^{0})=\left(\left<\xi_{1}f-\sigma(\partial_{1}f),\ldots,\xi_{n}f-\sigma(\partial_{n}f)\right>:\left<f\right>^{\infty}+\left<\sigma\right>\right)\cap\mathbb{Q}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n}].

By [38, Theorem 9.1] we have that the variety Wf0W_{f}^{0} is the characteristic variety of the ideal AnnD​(fλ)\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(f^{\lambda}), or in symbols:

(23) Wf0=Char⁡(AnnD​(fλ)).W_{f}^{0}=\mathrm{Char}(\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(f^{\lambda})).
Example 3.10.

Like in Example 3.8, let f=x2​z−y2f=x^{2}z-y^{2} be the defining equation for the Whitney umbrella. The ideal defining Wf0W_{f}^{0} before eliminating ss is

⟨ξ⁡(x2​z−y2)−s⁡(2​x​z),η⁡(x2​z−y2)−s⁡(−2​y),ζ⁡(x2​z−y2)−s⁡(x2)⟩:⟨x2​z−y2⟩∞+⟨s⟩=\displaystyle\left<\xi(x^{2}z-y^{2})-s(2xz),\,\eta(x^{2}z-y^{2})-s(-2y),\,\zeta(x^{2}z-y^{2})-s(x^{2})\right>:\left<x^{2}z-y^{2}\right>^{\infty}+\left<s\right>=

and eliminating ss gives

3.3.2. Computing Wf0W_{f}^{0} via a Blow-up

Fix a polynomial f∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] and let BlJac⁡(f)​ℂn{\rm Bl}_{{\rm Jac}(f)}\mathbb{C}^{n} be the blow-up of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} along the ideal defined by

Jac⁡(f)=⟨∂f∂x1,⋯,∂f∂xn⟩.{\rm Jac}(f)=\langle\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}},\cdots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}}\rangle.

In other words, BlJac⁡(f)​X{\rm Bl}_{{\rm Jac}(f)}X is the variety obtained as the closure of the graph of the rational map defined by the the generators of Jac⁡(f){\rm Jac}(f):

(24) BlJac⁡(f)​X:={(x,ξ)|x∈(X−𝐕(Jac(f))),ξ=Jac(f(x))}¯⊂X×ℙn−1.{\rm Bl}_{{\rm Jac}(f)}X:=\overline{\{(x,\xi)\;|\;x\in(X-\mathbf{V}(\mathrm{Jac}(f))),\;\;\xi=\mathrm{Jac}(f(x))\}}\subset X\times\mathbb{P}^{n-1}.

Let EE be the the exceptional divisor of this blow-up, that is E=BlJac⁡(f)​X∩𝐕⁡(Jac⁡(f))E={\rm Bl}_{{\rm Jac}(f)}X\cap\mathbf{V}({\rm Jac}(f)), and take Λα\Lambda_{\alpha}, α=2,…,r\alpha=2,\dots,r, to be the irreducible components of EE with Cα=π⁡(Λα)C_{\alpha}=\pi(\Lambda_{\alpha}).

By [47, Théorème 3.3] we have the equality

(25) Wf0=𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(0)∪𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(𝐕⁡(f))​⋃α=2rΛα.W_{f}^{0}=\mathbf{Con}(0)\cup\mathbf{Con}(\mathbf{V}(f))\bigcup_{\alpha=2}^{r}\Lambda_{\alpha}.

Hence in particular we may compute Wf0W_{f}^{0} directly from the exceptional divisor EE in a straightforward manner.

3.4. The Characteristic Variety of An Annihilator Module of a Product of Elements

The DD-module corresponding to the integral (1) is in fact associated to the annihilator ideal for a product of polynomials, rather than for the single polynomial case considered in the previous section. It has been shown by Sabbah [48] and Gyoja [49] that the Bernstein-Sato construction for one polynomial can be generalized to a product of several polynomials. For 𝒔=(s1,…,sp)\bm{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{p}) we define D⁡[𝒔]:=D⊗ℂℂ⁡[𝒔]D[\bm{s}]:=D\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}[\bm{s}] and for a product of polynomials we define the parametric annihilator ideal

AnnD⁡[𝒔](f1s1⋯fpsp):={P(𝒔)∈D[𝒔]|P(𝒔)∙f1s1⋯fpsp=0}.\mathrm{Ann}_{D[\bm{s}]}(f_{1}^{s_{1}}\cdots f_{p}^{s_{p}}):=\{P(\bm{s})\in D[\bm{s}]\,|\,P(\bm{s})\bullet f_{1}^{s_{1}}\cdots f_{p}^{s_{p}}=0\}.

We denote by 𝒩\mathscr{N} the associated DD-module D[𝒔]/AnnD⁡[𝒔](f1s1⋯fpsp)D[\bm{s}]/\mathrm{Ann}_{D[\bm{s}]}(f_{1}^{s_{1}}\cdots f_{p}^{s_{p}}) and its specialization to a fixed 𝝀=(λ1,…,λp)∈ℂp\bm{\lambda}=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{p})\in\mathbb{C}^{p} as 𝒩𝝀:=𝒩/((s1−λ1)​𝒩+⋯+(sp−λp)​𝒩)\mathscr{N}_{\bm{\lambda}}:=\mathscr{N}/((s_{1}-\lambda_{1})\mathscr{N}+\cdots+(s_{p}-\lambda_{p})\mathscr{N}). As in the case with one variable, for generic 𝝀\bm{\lambda} we have

𝒩𝝀≃D/AnnD(f1λ1⋯fpλp).\mathscr{N}_{\bm{\lambda}}\simeq D/\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(f_{1}^{\lambda_{1}}\cdots f_{p}^{\lambda_{p}}).

Using the multivariate Bernstein-Sato polynomial the genericity assumption for this isomorphism can be relaxed to an assumption of similar flavor as Theorem 3.5. This means that there exists an integer NN large enough so that fixing λ1=⋯=λp=−N\lambda_{1}=\cdots=\lambda_{p}=-N is generic enough and

D/AnnD(f1λ1⋯fpλp)≃D/AnnD(F−N)D/\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(f_{1}^{\lambda_{1}}\cdots f_{p}^{\lambda_{p}})\simeq D/\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(F^{-N})

where F:=f1⋯fpF:=f_{1}\cdots f_{p}. Let Y=𝐕⁡(F)Y=\mathbf{V}(F) and 𝒪X[∗Y]\mathscr{O}_{X}[*Y] denote the sheaf of holomorphic functions with singularities along YY, then

D/AnnD(F−N)≃𝒪X[∗Y].D/\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(F^{-N})\simeq\mathscr{O}_{X}[*Y].

By [47, Theorem 3.1] we get the characteristic varieties for generic 𝝀\bm{\lambda}

(26) Char(𝒩𝝀)=Char(𝒪X[∗Y])=WF0\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{N}_{\bm{\lambda}})=\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{O}_{X}[*Y])=W_{F}^{0}

where WF0W_{F}^{0} is defined in Definition 3.9 and can be calculated using the blow-up procedure described in the previous section.

4. Constructible Functions and Sheaves

We will now switch our point of view to the solutions of the system of PDEs represented by the DD-module. These solutions will be described by sheaves for which we recommend [50, 51] and the classical work [52]. In the general setting we define the solution complex

(27) S​o​l​(ℳ):=R​ℋ​o​m𝒟X​(ℳ,𝒪X)​[n]Sol(\mathscr{M}):=R\mathscr{H}om_{\mathscr{D}_{X}}(\mathscr{M},\mathscr{O}_{X})[n]

where the elements of degree zero correspond to the classical solutions of the PDE. It is a fundamental philosophy of the theory that we can go rather freely between a DD-module and its solution sheaf. This is formalized in the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence [53, 54, 55] showing that the category of regular holonomic DD-modules is equivalent to the category of perverse sheaves. In particular we have for holonomic DD-modules:

Theorem 4.1 ([50, Theorem 5.3.2]).

Let ℳ\mathscr{M} be a holonomic DD-module. With the notations above we have that C​C​(S​o​l​(ℳ))=C​C​(ℳ)CC(Sol(\mathscr{M}))=CC(\mathscr{M}) and Char⁡(ℳ)=Char⁡(S​o​l​(ℳ))\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M})=\mathrm{Char}(Sol(\mathscr{M})).

We will now define what we mean by the characteristic cycle of a complex of sheaves. Let ℱ∙\mathscr{F}^{\bullet} be a constructible sheaf on the algebraic variety XX with respect to the Whitney stratification {Sα}\{S_{\alpha}\}. For a regular map g:X→Yg:X\to Y between algebraic varieties, let Φg​(ℱ∙)\Phi_{g}(\mathscr{F}^{\bullet}) denote the vanishing cycles as defined by Delign [56]. The characteristic cycle of ℱ∙\mathscr{F}^{\bullet} is the Lagrangian cycle in T∗​XT^{*}X given by

(28) C​C​(ℱ∙):=∑αmα​𝐂𝐨𝐧​(Sα).CC(\mathscr{F}^{\bullet}):=\sum_{\alpha}m_{\alpha}\mathbf{Con}(S_{\alpha}).

Let x∈Sαx\in S_{\alpha} be a point and gg a generic function in a neighborhood of xx such that gg is zero on XαX_{\alpha} and (x,d​g​(x))∈TSα∗​X(x,dg(x))\in T_{S_{\alpha}}^{*}X then the coefficient mαm_{\alpha} is given by

(29) mα​(ℱ∙)=−χ⁡((Φg​(ℱ∙))x)m_{\alpha}(\mathscr{F}^{\bullet})=-\chi((\Phi_{g}(\mathscr{F}^{\bullet}))_{x})

i.e. minus the Euler characteristic of the stalk of Φg​(ℱ∙)\Phi_{g}(\mathscr{F}^{\bullet}) at xx. This Euler characteristic can be calculated more easily via stratified Morse theory. For a point p=(x,ξ)∈TSα∗​Xp=(x,\xi)\in T_{S_{\alpha}}^{*}X let N​M​D​(ℱ∙,p)NMD(\mathscr{F}^{\bullet},p) be the normal Morse data [31, Definition 3.6.1] and denote by C​LX​(x)CL_{X}(x) the complex link [31, Part I, Sec. 2.2] of x∈Sαx\in S_{\alpha}, then we have the equality

(30) −χ⁡((Φg​(ℱ∙))x)=χ⁡(N​M​D​(ℱ∙,p))=1−χ⁡(C​LX​(x)),-\chi((\Phi_{g}(\mathscr{F}^{\bullet}))_{x})=\chi(NMD(\mathscr{F}^{\bullet},p))=1-\chi(CL_{X}(x)),

hence in particular mα​(ℱx∙)=1−χ⁡(C​LX​(x))m_{\alpha}(\mathscr{F}_{x}^{\bullet})=1-\chi(CL_{X}(x)).

For a holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module ℳ\mathscr{M} we define the index [30] as

(31) χℳ​(x):=∑i(−1)i​dimℰ​x​t𝒟Xi​(ℳ,𝒪X)x.\chi_{\mathscr{M}}(x):=\sum_{i}(-1)^{i}\dim\mathscr{E}xt_{\mathscr{D}_{X}}^{i}(\mathscr{M},\,\mathscr{O}_{X})_{x}.

Let X∘⊂XX_{\circ}\subset X be a dense set such that X¯∘=X\overline{X}_{\circ}=X and X−X0X-X_{0} is the singular locus of ℳ\mathscr{M}. Then dimℰ​x​t𝒟Xi​(ℳ,𝒪X)x=0\dim\mathscr{E}xt_{\mathscr{D}_{X}}^{i}(\mathscr{M},\,\mathscr{O}_{X})_{x}=0 for i>0i>0 and x∈X∘x\in X_{\circ} [57, Corollary 4.4]. The index is therefore localized at i=0i=0 and since ℰ​x​t𝒟X0​(ℳ,𝒪X)=ℋ​o​m𝒟X​(ℳ,𝒪X)\mathscr{E}xt^{0}_{\mathscr{D}_{X}}(\mathscr{M},\mathscr{O}_{X})=\mathscr{H}om_{\mathscr{D}_{X}}(\mathscr{M},\mathscr{O}_{X}) we have

(32) χℳ​(x)=dimℋ​o​m𝒟X​(ℳ,𝒪X),\chi_{\mathscr{M}}(x)=\dim\mathscr{H}om_{\mathscr{D}_{X}}(\mathscr{M},\mathscr{O}_{X}),

i.e. the index at a generic point is just the dimension of the solution space of the 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module, sometimes referred to as the rank of the 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module. The index can also be defined for a complex of sheaves ℱ∙\mathscr{F}^{\bullet} as the the Euler characteristic of the stalks: χ⁡(ℱx∙)=∑i(−1)i​dimℋi​(ℱx∙)\chi(\mathscr{F}_{x}^{\bullet})=\sum_{i}(-1)^{i}\dim\mathscr{H}^{i}(\mathscr{F}_{x}^{\bullet}) and these numbers coincides if ℱ∙=R​ℋ​o​m𝒟X​(ℳ,𝒪X)\mathscr{F}^{\bullet}=R\mathscr{H}om_{\mathscr{D}_{X}}(\mathscr{M},\mathscr{O}_{X}).

For a constructible complex of sheaves Kashiwara-Dubson’s index theorem states [30, 32, 33]

(33) χ⁡(ℱx∙)=∑α(−1)dα​mα​𝐄𝐮S¯α​(x),\chi(\mathscr{F}_{x}^{\bullet})=\sum_{\alpha}(-1)^{d_{\alpha}}m_{\alpha}\mathbf{Eu}_{\overline{S}_{\alpha}}(x),

with 𝐄𝐮\mathbf{Eu} being the Euler obstruction from (6).

Let YY be a hypersurface defined by F=0F=0 where F=f1⋯fpF=f_{1}\cdots f_{p} and let 𝒪X[∗Y]\mathscr{O}_{X}[*Y] denote the sheaf of holomorphic functions with singularities along YY. This sheaf sits in the exact sequence

(34) 0→𝒪X→𝒪X[∗Y]→𝒪X[∗Y]/𝒪X→00\to\mathscr{O}_{X}\to\mathscr{O}_{X}[*Y]\to\mathscr{O}_{X}[*Y]/\mathscr{O}_{X}\to 0

and using e.g. [58, Theorem 2.2.3] or [52, Theorem 9.4.5] we have

CC(𝒪X[∗Y])=CC(𝒪X)+CC(𝒪X[∗Y]/𝒪X).CC(\mathscr{O}_{X}[*Y])=CC(\mathscr{O}_{X})+CC(\mathscr{O}_{X}[*Y]/\mathscr{O}_{X}).

At the moment we view this as an equality between characteristic cycles of DD-modules. To use Theorem 4.1 we first need the solution complexes. Note that, by [59, Theorem 1.1], we have

Rℋom𝒟X(𝒪X,𝒪X)=ℂXandRℋom𝒟X(𝒪X[∗Y]/𝒪X,𝒪X)=ℂY[−1].R\mathscr{H}om_{\mathscr{D}_{X}}(\mathscr{O}_{X},\,\mathscr{O}_{X})=\mathbb{C}_{X}\ \mathrm{and}\ R\mathscr{H}om_{\mathscr{D}_{X}}(\mathscr{O}_{X}[*Y]/\mathscr{O}_{X},\,\mathscr{O}_{X})=\mathbb{C}_{Y}[-1].

Shifting these by nn to obtain the solution complexes and using C​C​(ℱ∙​[k])=(−1)k​C​C​(ℱ∙)CC(\mathscr{F}^{\bullet}[k])=(-1)^{k}CC(\mathscr{F}^{\bullet}) we find

(35) C​C​(𝒩𝝀)=𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(0)+C​C​(ℂY​[d])CC(\mathscr{N}_{\bm{\lambda}})=\mathbf{Con}(0)+CC(\mathbb{C}_{Y}[d])

for generic 𝝀∈ℂp\bm{\lambda}\in\mathbb{C}^{p} and d=dimY=n−1d=\dim Y=n-1. Applying the index theorem to ℂY​[d]\mathbb{C}_{Y}[d] and using χ⁡(ℂY​[d]x)=(−1)d\chi(\mathbb{C}_{Y}[d]_{x})=(-1)^{d} we obtain

(36) 𝟙Y​(x)=∑α(−1)d−dα​mα​𝐄𝐮S¯α​(x),\mathbb{1}_{Y}(x)=\sum_{\alpha}(-1)^{d-d_{\alpha}}m_{\alpha}\mathbf{Eu}_{\overline{S}_{\alpha}}(x),

where 𝟙Y\mathbb{1}_{Y} is the characteristic function of YY. In particular this means

(37) C​C​(𝒩𝝀)=𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(0)+∑αmα​𝐂𝐨𝐧​(Sα).CC(\mathscr{N}_{\bm{\lambda}})=\mathbf{Con}(0)+\sum_{\alpha}m_{\alpha}\mathbf{Con}(S_{\alpha}).

The strata that appear in this cycle with non-zero mαm_{\alpha} are precisely given by the blow-up procedure in Section 3.3.2. However, an alternative (and potentially faster) method that also gives us the multiplicities mαm_{\alpha} explicitly is calculating a Whitney stratification of YY, calculating the Euler obstructions using polar multiplicities (see (11)) and finally solving the linear system (36). We explain in more detail how this can be used in practice in the remark below.

Remark 4.2 (Calculating the Euler Characteristic of the Complex Link).

Consider a complex variety Y=𝐕⁡(f1,…,fs)⊂ℂnY=\mathbf{V}(f_{1},\dots,f_{s})\subset\mathbb{C}^{n} of dimension d=dim(Y)d=\dim(Y) and let Y={Sα}Y=\{S_{\alpha}\} be a Whitney stratification of YY. Obviously a key step in this calculation is the computation of a Whitney stratification of YY, this is made possible by the recent algorithms of [26, 22]. Starting with only the defining equations f1,…,fsf_{1},\dots,f_{s} of the variety YY the procedure is as follows:

    We note that in the construction of the matrix above, if Sα⊄S¯βS_{\alpha}\not\subset\overline{S}_{\beta} then we have 𝐄𝐮S¯β​(Sα)=0\mathbf{Eu}_{\overline{S}_{\beta}}(S_{\alpha})=0. Supposing Sα⊂S¯βS_{\alpha}\subset\overline{S}_{\beta} we employ (11) to compute the integer 𝐄𝐮S¯β​(Sα)\mathbf{Eu}_{\overline{S}_{\beta}}(S_{\alpha}); this requires the following calculations:

    • •

      Compute the polar varieties Pk​(S¯β)P_{k}(\overline{S}_{\beta}) for k=dα+1,…,dβk=d_{\alpha}+1,\dots,d_{\beta} using (5).

    • •

      Compute the multiplicities multS¯α​(Pk​(S¯β))\mathrm{mult}_{\overline{S}_{\alpha}}(P_{k}(\overline{S}_{\beta})) using, e.g., the algorithm of [23], as implemented in [61].

  3. (3)

    (11)=𝐄𝐮⁡(Y)​(mα1mαr),\begin{pmatrix}1\\ \vdots\\ 1\end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{Eu}(Y)\begin{pmatrix}m_{\alpha_{1}}\\ \vdots\\ m_{\alpha_{r}}\end{pmatrix},

    hence we obtain the multiplicities mαim_{\alpha_{i}} by solving the integer linear system above.

  4. (4)

    χ⁡(C​LY​(Sαi))=1−(−1)d−dα​mαi\chi(CL_{Y}(S_{\alpha_{i}}))=1-(-1)^{d-d_{\alpha}}m_{\alpha_{i}}

    for each strata SαiS_{\alpha_{i}}.

♠\spadesuit

We note that it is only strata from the unique coarsest Whitney stratification that can appear with non-zero multiplicity in the characteristic cycle of 𝟙Y\mathbb{1}_{Y}, as is proved in the proposition below.

Proposition 4.3.

If {Sα}\{S_{\alpha}\} is a non-minimal Whitney stratification containing the unnecessary strata Sβ{S}_{\beta} which does not appear in the unique minimal Whitney stratification, then mβ=0m_{\beta}=0 in the decomposition (36).

Proof.

Let xx be a (smooth) point in SβS_{\beta}. Since (36) holds for any Whitney stratification, especially the minimal one, we have

(38) 𝟙Y​(x)=∑γ(−1)d−dγ​mγ​𝐄𝐮S¯γ​(x)=1,\mathbb{1}_{Y}(x)=\sum_{\gamma}(-1)^{d-d_{\gamma}}m_{\gamma}\mathbf{Eu}_{\overline{S}_{\gamma}}(x)=1,

where we sum over S¯γ\overline{S}_{\gamma} lying above S¯β\overline{S}_{\beta} in the flag. Including the variety S¯β\overline{S}_{\beta} we obtain

(39) 1=𝟙Y​(x)=(−1)d−dβ​mβ​𝐄𝐮S¯β​(x)+∑γ(−1)d−dγ​mγ​𝐄𝐮S¯γ​(x)=(−1)d−dβ​mβ+1.1=\mathbb{1}_{Y}(x)=(-1)^{d-d_{\beta}}m_{\beta}\mathbf{Eu}_{\overline{S}_{\beta}}(x)+\sum_{\gamma}(-1)^{d-d_{\gamma}}m_{\gamma}\mathbf{Eu}_{\overline{S}_{\gamma}}(x)=(-1)^{d-d_{\beta}}m_{\beta}+1.

Which is true only if mβ=0m_{\beta}=0. ∎

Before showing some examples of calculating characteristic cycles we give some examples of just the Euler obstructions.

Example 4.4.

(A) For a curve the Euler obstructions are just the multiplicities of the points on the curve. For the curve in Figure 2(a) every point is smooth (i.e. Euler obstruction one) except the origin where the multiplicity and therefore the Euler obstruction is two. For curves the polar multiplicity coincides with the standard multiplicity.

(B) For a surface xn+yp​zq=0x^{n}+y^{p}z^{q}=0 with gcd⁡(n,p,q)=1\mathrm{gcd}(n,p,q)=1 we have 𝐄𝐮Y​(0)=min⁡(n,p)+min⁡(n,q)−n\mathbf{Eu}_{Y}(0)=\min(n,p)+\min(n,q)-n (see e.g. [30]). In the case of Figure 2(b) we have 𝐄𝐮Y​(0)=3\mathbf{Eu}_{Y}(0)=3

(C) For a hypersurface in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} with isolated singularities the Euler obstructions can be obtained from the Milnor number at the singularity. If xx is the singular point then 𝐄𝐮Y​(x)=1+(−1)n​μ\mathbf{Eu}_{Y}(x)=1+(-1)^{n}\mu where μ\mu is the Milnor number associated to a generic hyperplane section of YY containing xx, see e.g. [50, Example 4.1.35]. For the surface in Figure 2(c) this number is one so the Euler obstruction at the singular points vanishes. Calculating the polar multiplicities at one of these points we find {0,2,2}\{0,2,2\} so indeed 𝐄𝐮Y​(x)=0\mathbf{Eu}_{Y}(x)=0. ⋄\diamond

where πN:T∗​N→N\pi_{N}:T^{*}N\to N is the canonical projection. The morphism φd\varphi_{d} is the dual of the differential of φ\varphi which maps Tx​M→Tφ⁡(x)​MT_{x}M\to T_{\varphi(x)}M. Together with the canonical projection φπ\varphi_{\pi}

(47) φπ:M×NT∗​N→T∗​N\varphi_{\pi}:M\times_{N}T^{*}N\to T^{*}N

we have the commutative diagram:

On the level of Lagrangian cycles, φπ∗φd∗\varphi_{\pi*}\varphi_{d}^{*} is a group homomorphism mapping Lagrangian cycles in T∗​MT^{*}M with respect to 𝒮\mathcal{S} to Lagrangian cycles in T∗​NT^{*}N with respect to 𝒯\mathcal{T}. 5.1. Integration of Distributions

In this section we are interested in the integration of regular holonomic distributions.

Definition 5.2.

A distribution uu is said to be regular holonomic if its annihilator ideal defines a regular holonomic DD-module.

As every regular holonomic distribution is tempered (cf. [63]), they can always be extended to projective space ℝxn×ℝzm↪ℙxn×ℝzm\mathbb{R}_{x}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}_{z}^{m}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}_{x}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}_{z}^{m} so that the projection φ:ℙxn×ℝzm→ℝzm:(x,z)↦z\varphi:\mathbb{P}_{x}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}_{z}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}_{z}^{m}\,:\,(x,z)\mapsto z is proper. If u⁡(x,z)u(x,z) is a regular holonomic distribution on ℝn×ℝm\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}, there exists a sheaf of left ideals ℐ\mathscr{I} of 𝒟ℙn×ℂm\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{P}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{m}} such that 𝒟ℙn×ℂm/ℐ\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{P}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{m}}/\mathscr{I} is a sheaf of regular holonomic 𝒟ℙn×ℂm\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{P}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{m}}-modules. If HH is any hyperplane and we identify ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} with ℙn−H\mathbb{P}^{n}-H, then ℐ|ℂn×ℂm\mathscr{I}|_{\mathbb{C}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{m}} is equal to the sheaf of left ideals in 𝒟ℂn×ℂm\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{C}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{m}} annihilating uu. Using [64, Proposition 5] there is a global section uhu_{h} in Hom𝒟ℙn×ℂn​(𝒟ℙn×ℂm/ℐ,𝒟′​(ℙn×ℂm))\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{P}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{n}}}(\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{P}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{m}}/\mathscr{I},\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{P}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{m})) extending uu. This means that we identify the integration of uu against the measure d​x/xdx/x with the integration of uhu_{h} against the canonical one-form Ω\Omega given by

Ω=∑i=0n(−1)n−1−i​d​x0/x0∧⋯∧d​xi^/xi∧⋯∧d​xn/xn.\Omega=\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^{n-1-i}dx_{0}/x_{0}\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{dx_{i}}/x_{i}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_{n}/x_{n}.

This identification is well-known in the physics literature where it goes under the Cheng-Wu theorem [1, Chapter 2, Theorem 1]. We therefore make the identification between the following pairings

⟨∫ℝnu​d​xx,ϕ⁡(x,z)⟩:=⟨∫ℙnuh​Ω,ϕh​(x0,x,z)⟩:=⟨φ∗​(uh),ϕh⟩=⟨uh,φ∗​(ϕh)⟩\left<\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}u\frac{dx}{x},\,\phi(x,z)\right>:=\left<\int_{\mathbb{P}^{n}}u_{h}\,\Omega,\,\phi_{h}(x_{0},x,z)\right>:=\left<\varphi_{*}(u_{h}),\phi_{h}\right>=\left<u_{h},\,\varphi^{*}(\phi_{h})\right>

where ϕ\phi is a function with rapid decrease in the Schwartz space 𝒮⁡(ℝxn×ℝzm)\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}_{x}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}_{z}^{m}), ϕh\phi_{h} its homogenization in xx and uhu_{h} contains a factor x0ν0x_{0}^{\nu_{0}} where ν0\nu_{0} is fixed by projective invariance.

As our objective is to make sense of the integral (1) and in particular the Feynman integral in Lee-Pomeransky form:

(51) ∫ℝ+nx1ν1⋯xnνn(f⁡(x,z)−i​0)λ​d​x1x1∧⋯∧d​xnxn,\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}}\frac{x_{1}^{\nu_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{\nu_{n}}}{(f(x,z)-i0)^{\lambda}}\frac{dx_{1}}{x_{1}}\wedge\cdots\wedge\frac{dx_{n}}{x_{n}},

we have to make sure that the integrand can be understood as a regular holonomic distribution so that the above construction applies.

We first change the integration domain from ℝ+n\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n} to ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} by defining the the tempered distribution

x+ν=xν​for​x>0,x+ν=0​for​x≤0.x_{+}^{\nu}=x^{\nu}\ \mathrm{for}\ x>0,\quad x_{+}^{\nu}=0\ \mathrm{for}\ x\leq 0.

In the Feynman integral the meaning of i​0i0 is as follows. Let ff be a polynomial with real coefficients. For a complex parameter λ\lambda we then define the distributions

(52) (f±i​0)λ:=f+λ+e±i​π​λ​f−λ(f\pm i0)^{\lambda}:=f_{+}^{\lambda}+e^{\pm i\pi\lambda}f_{-}^{\lambda}

where

f+λ=fλ​for​f>0,f+λ=0​for​f≤0f_{+}^{\lambda}=f^{\lambda}\ \mathrm{for}\ f>0,\quad f_{+}^{\lambda}=0\ \mathrm{for}\ f\leq 0

and similarly

f−λ=0​for​f≥0,f−λ=|f|λ​for​f<0.f_{-}^{\lambda}=0\ \mathrm{for}\ f\geq 0,\quad f_{-}^{\lambda}=|f|^{\lambda}\ \mathrm{for}\ f<0.

For Re​λ>0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda>0 the right-hand side in (52) has polynomial growth and is thus well-defined as a tempered distribution. Both of the distributions x+νx_{+}^{\nu} and f+λf_{+}^{\lambda} can be extended to an entire analytic function of ν\nu and λ\lambda by renormalizing them with a certain product of Γ\Gamma-functions coming from their Bernstein-Sato polynomial [65, Lemma 2.10].

Distributions can famously not always be multiplied. A sufficient condition for multiplication to be allowed is given by Hörmander’s product theorem [41, Theorem 8.5.3], this condition states that the product of two distributions uu and vv can be well-defined if there exists no points (x,ξ)∈W​FA​(u),(y,η)∈W​FA​(v)(x,\xi)\in WF_{A}(u),\ (y,\eta)\in WF_{A}(v) such that x=yx=y and ξ+η=0\xi+\eta=0 (the colloquial term for this phenomenon is that the wave fronts collide). The analytic wave front sets for our distributions of interest are

(53) W​FA​((x±i​0)ν)\displaystyle WF_{A}((x\pm i0)^{\nu}) ⊆{(0;ξ)|ξ≷0},W​FA​(x±ν)⊆{(0;ξ)|ξ∈ℝ∖0},\displaystyle\subseteq\{(0;\,\xi)\,|\,\xi\gtrless 0\},\qquad WF_{A}(x_{\pm}^{\nu})\subseteq\{(0;\xi)\,|\,\xi\in\mathbb{R}\setminus 0\},
(54) W​FA​(1(f±i​0)λ)\displaystyle WF_{A}\left(\frac{1}{(f\pm i0)^{\lambda}}\right) ⊆⋃α𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(Sα),\displaystyle\subseteq\bigcup_{\alpha}\mathbf{Con}(S_{\alpha}),

where ∪Sα\cup S_{\alpha} is the subset of the Whitney stratification of the hypersurface 𝐕⁡(f)\mathbf{V}(f) appearing with non-zero multiplicity in (8). It is not hard to construct examples where the analytic wave front sets of the integrand in (51) collide. Take e.g. ff to be the polynomial defining the Whitney umbrella, see Example 3.8, there all three strata have colliding points with those in W​FA​(xi+ν)WF_{A}(x_{i+}^{\nu}).

It is clear from Theorem 3.6 that all distributions in the integrand are regular holonomic. In [66, Theorem 1] it was claimed without proof that this product is well-defined. A more general theorem with a proof was given in [65, Theorem 2.11]. This theorem both tell us that (i) the product is well-defined and defines a regular holonomic distribution and (ii), that the characteristic variety of the annihilator module of the product is given by (this follows from Equation (26) for generic λ\lambda)

(55) Char⁡(AnnD​(fλ1​gλ2))=Char⁡(AnnD​((f⋅g)λ))\mathrm{Char}(\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(f^{\lambda_{1}}g^{\lambda_{2}}))=\mathrm{Char}(\mathrm{Ann}_{D}((f\cdot g)^{\lambda}))

for generic fixed complex numbers λi\lambda_{i}.

5.2. Integration module

We again work in the setting described at the beginning of this Section (Section 5). Let II be a DD-ideal, let {x1,…,xn,z1,…,zm}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}\} local coordinates on MM and let {z1,…,zm}\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}\} local coordinates on NN. Define the left DND_{N} and right DMD_{M} bimodule DN←M:D_{N\leftarrow M}:

DN←M:=DM/(∂1DM+⋯+∂nDM).D_{N\leftarrow M}:=D_{M}/(\partial_{1}D_{M}+\cdots+\partial_{n}D_{M}).

We then define the integration module as the tensor product

(56) DN←M⊗DMDM/I≃DM/(I+∂1DM+⋯+∂nDM)D_{N\leftarrow M}\otimes_{D_{M}}D_{M}/I\simeq D_{M}/(I+\partial_{1}D_{M}+\cdots+\partial_{n}D_{M})

with the integration ideal being

(57) (I+∂1DM+⋯+∂nDM)∩DN.(I+\partial_{1}D_{M}+\cdots+\partial_{n}D_{M})\cap D_{N}.

We note that the integral of a regular holonomic DD-module is again a regular holonomic DD-module, [36, Theorem 5.5.3]. Given a morphism of manifolds φ:M→N\varphi:M\to N we will denote the integral of a DD-module ℳ\mathscr{M} on MM along the fibres of φ\varphi by ∫φℳ\int_{\varphi}\mathscr{M}. In [38] Kashiwara proves the following theorem (see also [58, Remark 2.5.2]).

Theorem 5.3 (Kashiwara, [38], Theorem 4.27).

Let φ:M→N\varphi:M\to N be a morphism of manifolds and ℳ\mathscr{M} a regular holonomic DMD_{M}-module such that φ\varphi is proper on Supp​ℳ→N\mathrm{Supp}\,\mathscr{M}\to N. Then

(58) Char⁡(∫φℳ)⊂φπ​φd−1​Char​(ℳ).\mathrm{Char}\left(\int_{\varphi}\mathscr{M}\right)\subset\varphi_{\pi}\varphi_{d}^{-1}\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M}).
Remark 5.4.

From [38, page 79] we have that equality holds in the above theorem if

φπ:φd−1​Char​(ℳ)→T∗​N\varphi_{\pi}:\varphi_{d}^{-1}\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M})\to T^{*}N

is finite. We will establish that this is fact always the case in our setting in Lemma 5.5 below. ♠\spadesuit

In the special case of Euler-Mellin integrals, we can identify M=ℙxn×ℂzmM=\mathbb{P}^{n}_{x}\times\mathbb{C}^{m}_{z} and N=ℂzmN=\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m} with φ\varphi being the canonical projection The commutative diagram (48) now becomes

(59)

For the integral (1) we first define the annihilator module of the integrand

𝒩𝝀,𝝂=Dℂn×ℂm/AnnDℂn×ℂm(x1ν1⋯xnνnf1−λ1⋯fp−λp)\mathscr{N}_{\bm{\lambda},\bm{\nu}}=D_{\mathbb{C}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{m}}/\mathrm{Ann}_{D_{\mathbb{C}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{m}}}(x_{1}^{\nu_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{\nu_{n}}f_{1}^{-\lambda_{1}}\cdots f_{p}^{-\lambda_{p}})

and then by the construction in the beginning of Section 5.1 we lift this to a module on ℙn×ℂm\mathbb{P}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{m} generated by the annihilator of the product of homogenization of all the fif_{i} and x0ν0⋯x1ν1x_{0}^{\nu_{0}}\cdots x_{1}^{\nu_{1}}.

In practice this means to calculate the characteristic variety of the integration ideal we simply have to calculate the fibre of φd−1\varphi_{d}^{-1} and eliminate the integration variables and their corresponding cotangent variables. Explicitly we have that

(60) 𝐈⁡(φd−1​Char​(ℳ))=(𝐈⁡(Char⁡(ℳ))+⟨ξ0,…,ξn⟩)∩ℚ⁡[x0,…,xn,z1,…,zm,ζ1,…,ζm]\mathbf{I}(\varphi_{d}^{-1}\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M}))=(\mathbf{I}(\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M}))+\left<\xi_{0},\ldots,\xi_{n}\right>)\cap\mathbb{Q}[x_{0},\dots,x_{n},z_{1},\ldots,z_{m},\zeta_{1},\ldots,\zeta_{m}]

hence to obtain φπ​φd−1​Char​(ℳ)\varphi_{\pi}\varphi_{d}^{-1}\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M}) we just have to calculate (the radical of) the ideal

(𝐈⁡(Char⁡(ℳ))+⟨ξ0,…,ξn⟩)∩ℚ⁡[z1,…,zm,ζ1,…,ζm].(\mathbf{I}(\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M}))+\left<\xi_{0},\ldots,\xi_{n}\right>)\cap\mathbb{Q}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{m},\zeta_{1},\ldots,\zeta_{m}].

We now show that the assertion of Remark 5.4 holds in our case of interest.

Lemma 5.5.

Let φ:ℙxn×ℂzm→ℂzm\varphi:\mathbb{P}^{n}_{x}\times\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m}\to\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m} be the canonical projection and let ℳ\mathscr{M} be a regular holonomic DMD_{M}-module. Then

(61) Char⁡(∫φℳ)=φπ​φd−1​Char​(ℳ).\mathrm{Char}(\int_{\varphi}\mathscr{M})=\varphi_{\pi}\varphi_{d}^{-1}\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M}).
Proof.

Note that by Remark 5.4 it is enough to show that φπ:φd−1​Char​(ℳ)→ℂzm×ℙˇζm−1\varphi_{\pi}:\varphi_{d}^{-1}\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M})\to\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m}\times\check{\mathbb{P}}_{\zeta}^{m-1} is a finite map; recall a map is finite if and only if it is proper and quasi-finite, i.e. proper and has finite fibers (see e.g. [67, Corollary 6.5]). Note φπ\varphi_{\pi} is proper as all fibers are projective varieties and hence compact. Hence it is enough to show that for each p∈φd−1​Char​(ℳ)p\in\varphi_{d}^{-1}\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M}) the fiber φπ−1​(φπ​(p))\varphi_{\pi}^{-1}(\varphi_{\pi}(p)) is finite; i.e. that the map φπ:φd−1​Char​(ℳ)→φπ​(φd−1​Char​(ℳ))\varphi_{\pi}:\varphi_{d}^{-1}\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M})\to{\varphi_{\pi}(\varphi_{d}^{-1}\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M}))} is a finite map. Now, since we only consider the map φπ\varphi_{\pi} onto its image it is dominant by construction, and by, e.g. [68, page 323], we know that a dominant map between complex varieties is finite if and only if it is proper, hence the conclusion follows. ∎

Remark 5.6 (Proof of Theorem A and Theorem B).

We note that the portion of the conclusions of Theorem A and Theorem B relating the characteristic variety of the integral (1) to that of the integrand follow directly from Lemma 5.5 above. The (implicit) statement in Theorem A that the characteristic variety associated to the integrand is given by the blowup construction follows from the discussions in Subsections 3.3.2 and 3.4 (in particular (26)). The (implicit) statement in Theorem B that the characteristic variety associated to the integrand is given by the computation of conormal varieties of Whitney strata and multiplicities follows from (26), and the discussions in Section 4, see in particular Remark 4.2 for the multiplicity portion. ♠\spadesuit

We will now show how to obtain not just the characteristic variety but in fact the full characteristic cycle of the DD-module annihilating the integral. As seen in Section 4 there is a close relationship between constructible functions and Lagrangian cycles, i.e. our characteristic cycles, this is actually an equivalence of categories proven by MacPherson [29].

Let Y⊂MY\subset M be a hypersurface defined defined by f=0f=0. In Section 4 we showed that the characteristic cycle of the annihilator ideal of ff is determined by YY, it follows directly that

(62) C​C​(AnnD​(fλ))=C​C​(𝟙M−𝟙Y).CC(\mathrm{Ann}_{D}(f^{\lambda}))=CC(\mathbb{1}_{M}-\mathbb{1}_{Y}).

With M=ℙxn×ℂzmM=\mathbb{P}_{x}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m}, φ\varphi being the canonical projection onto ℂzm\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m} and Y=𝐕(x0⋯xnF1⋯Fp)Y=\mathbf{V}(x_{0}\cdots x_{n}F_{1}\cdots F_{p}) we apply the proper push-forward from (50) we obtain

φ∗​(𝟙ℙn×ℂm−𝟙Y)​(z)=χ⁡((ℙn×ℂm)∩φ−1​(z))−χ⁡(Y∩φ−1​(z))=n+1−χ⁡(Y∩φ−1​(z)).\varphi_{*}(\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb{P}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{m}}-\mathbb{1}_{Y})(z)=\chi((\mathbb{P}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{m})\cap\varphi^{-1}(z))-\chi(Y\cap\varphi^{-1}(z))=n+1-\chi(Y\cap\varphi^{-1}(z)).

This constructible function is simply the index (31) of the integration module 𝒥=∫φ𝒩𝝀,𝝂\mathscr{J}=\int_{\varphi}\mathscr{N}_{\bm{\lambda},\bm{\nu}}. For a generic zz (especially outside the singular locus) this gives the rank, i.e. the dimension of the solution space, of this module.

Note that the integer rank⁡(𝒥)\mathrm{rank}(\mathscr{J}) is precisely the maximum likelihood degree [69] of 𝐕(x1⋯xnf1⋯fp)\mathbf{V}(x_{1}\cdots x_{n}f_{1}\cdots f_{p}), i.e. the Euler characteristic of its complement in the algebraic torus:

(63) rank(𝒥)=χ((ℂ∗)n−𝐕(x1⋯xnf1⋯fp)).\mathrm{rank}(\mathscr{J})=\chi((\mathbb{C}^{*})^{n}-\mathbf{V}(x_{1}\cdots x_{n}f_{1}\cdots f_{p})).

Let Z=Sing⁡(𝒥)⊂ℂzmZ={\rm Sing}(\mathscr{J})\subset\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m} be the singular locus of 𝒥\mathscr{J}. If πz:ℂzm×ℙζm−1→ℂzm\pi_{z}:\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m}\times\mathbb{P}_{\zeta}^{m-1}\to\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m} is the canonical projection, then Sing⁡(𝒥):=πz​(Char∗​(𝒥))¯\mathrm{Sing}(\mathscr{J}):=\overline{\pi_{z}(\mathrm{Char}^{*}(\mathscr{J}))}. Let {Wα}\{W_{\alpha}\} be a Whitney stratification of ZZ. To get the characteristic cycle we can again employ Kashiwara’s index theorem:

(64) χ𝒥​(z)=n+1−χ⁡(Y∩φ−1​(z))=rank⁡(𝒥)−∑α(−1)d−dα​μα​𝐄𝐮W¯α​(z),\chi_{\mathscr{J}}(z)=n+1-\chi(Y\cap\varphi^{-1}(z))=\mathrm{rank}(\mathscr{J})-\sum_{\alpha}(-1)^{d-d_{\alpha}}\mu_{\alpha}\mathbf{Eu}_{\overline{W}_{\alpha}}(z),

where μα\mu_{\alpha} is an integer (giving the multiplicity), dd is the dimension of the singular locus ZZ, and dα=dim(Wα).d_{\alpha}=\dim(W_{\alpha}). Since the Euler obstruction is constant on strata, the index χ𝒥​(z)\chi_{\mathscr{J}}(z) is also constant on strata. By ordering the strata by dimension this again leads to an upper-triangular system where we can solve for the μα\mu_{\alpha} explicitly. We give details as to how the values appearing in this computation may be carried our explicitly in below.

Finally, we note that (64) also implies [21, Theorem 5.1].

Remark 5.7 (Computing multiplicities for the characteristic cycle of the integral).

As above consider the polynomial G=x0⋯xnFhG=x_{0}\cdots x_{n}F_{h} in ℂ⁡[x,z]\mathbb{C}[x,z], where FhF_{h} is the homogenization of the product F=f1⋯fpF=f_{1}\cdots f_{p} in (1) with respect to the new variable x0x_{0}. Again take Y=𝐕⁡(G)⊂ℙxn×ℂzmY=\mathbf{V}(G)\subset\mathbb{P}_{x}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m}, let φ:ℙxn×ℂzm→ℂzm\varphi:\mathbb{P}_{x}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m}\to\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m} be the projection, and let ℳ\mathscr{M} denote the DD-module which annihilates the integral (1).

From either Theorem A or Theorem B we obtain the characteristic variety Char⁡(ℳ)⊂ℂzm×ℙζm−1\mathrm{Char}(\mathscr{M})\subset\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m}\times\mathbb{P}^{m-1}_{\zeta} of the integral. Considering the projection map πz:ℂzm×ℙζm−1→ℂzm\pi_{z}:\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m}\times\mathbb{P}^{m-1}_{\zeta}\to\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m} we have that the singular locus of ℳ\mathscr{M} is given by Z:=Sing⁡(ℳ)=πz​(Char∗​(ℳ))¯⊂ℂzmZ:={\rm Sing}(\mathscr{M})=\overline{\pi_{z}(\mathrm{Char}^{*}(\mathscr{M}))}\subset\mathbb{C}_{z}^{m} where Char∗​(ℳ)\mathrm{Char}^{*}(\mathscr{M}) denotes the characteristic variety with the zero-section removed. Let {Wi|i=1,…,ρ}\{W_{i}\;|i=1,\dots,\rho\}, Z=∪WiZ=\cup W_{i}, be a Whitney stratification of the algebraic variety Sing⁡(ℳ){\rm Sing}(\mathscr{M}) with some fixed ordering of strata. Set c(G):=χ((ℂ∗)n−𝐕(x1⋯xnf1(x,z0)⋯fp(x,z0)))−(n+1)c(G):=\chi((\mathbb{C}^{*})^{n}-\mathbf{V}(x_{1}\cdots x_{n}f_{1}(x,z_{0})\cdots f_{p}(x,z_{0})))-(n+1) where the polynomials fif_{i} are evaluated at a generic point z0z_{0} outside of the singular locus ZZ, and the xix_{i} are treated as variables with the Euler characteristic calculation taking place in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}.

Consider the problem of computing the multiplicities μα\mu_{\alpha} in (64). From (64) we can write down the linear system (given also above in (3)):

Using the procedure described in Remark 4.2 we can compute the integer matrix 𝐄𝐮⁡(Z)\mathbf{Eu}(Z). It remains to compute the integers c⁡(G)c(G) and χ⁡(Y∩φ−1​(zi))\chi(Y\cap\varphi^{-1}(z_{i})). We first note that the Euler characteristics of affine or projective complex varieties (and of Zariski open subsets of affine or projective varieties via the inclusion/exclusion property of Euler characteristics) may be computed with any algorithm to compute the Euler characteristic of a projective variety (e.g. [70], as implemented in [71]). Hence the main practical question remaining is how to deal with picking random ziz_{i} of the required type which can be effectively represented on a computer (i.e. most practical sampling methods deliver floating point numbers as output which can then not be used as input into the Euler characteristic calculation in a straightforward way).

First consider the integer χ((ℂ∗)n−𝐕(x1⋯xnf1(x,z0)⋯fp(x,z0)))\chi((\mathbb{C}^{*})^{n}-\mathbf{V}(x_{1}\cdots x_{n}f_{1}(x,z_{0})\cdots f_{p}(x,z_{0}))) appearing in c⁡(G)c(G); in this case, since we seek a general element z0z_{0} of ℂm\mathbb{C}^{m} not in ZZ we may simply choose a random vector of rational numbers (since ZZ is a proper subvariety of ℂm\mathbb{C}^{m}). Next consider the integers χ⁡(Y∩φ−1​(zi))\chi(Y\cap\varphi^{-1}(z_{i})), where ziz_{i} is a general element in WiW_{i}. Let IWiI_{W_{i}} denote the radical ideal defining Wi¯.\overline{W_{i}}. One remedy for this is as follows:

  1. (1)

    Take di=dim(Wi)d_{i}=\dim(W_{i}) general linear equations ℓj\ell_{j} defining the idea Li=⟨ℓ1,…,ℓdi⟩L_{i}=\langle\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{d_{i}}\rangle in ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z], so that 𝐕⁡(Li)\mathbf{V}(L_{i}) is a general linear space of codimension did_{i} in ℂzm\mathbb{C}^{m}_{z}. In practice we can construct ℓj\ell_{j} by taking random rational coefficients, and hence can represent LiL_{i} on a computer.

  2. (2)

    Compute the Euler characteristic of Y∩𝐕⁡(IWi+Li)Y\cap\mathbf{V}(I_{W_{i}}+L_{i}) where we abuse notation and consider the ideals IWiI_{W_{i}} and LiL_{i} both as ideals in ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z] and in ℂ⁡[x,z]\mathbb{C}[x,z]. Note that by construction 𝐕⁡(IWi+Li)⊂ℂzm\mathbf{V}(I_{W_{i}}+L_{i})\subset\mathbb{C}^{m}_{z}, considered as an variety in ℂzm\mathbb{C}^{m}_{z}, consists of exactly deg⁡(Wi¯)\deg(\overline{W_{i}}) many points; let Θi\Theta_{i} denote this finite set of deg⁡(Wi¯)\deg(\overline{W_{i}}) many general points in WiW_{i}. It follows that Y∩𝐕⁡(IWi+Li)=Y∩φ−1​(Θi)Y\cap\mathbf{V}(I_{W_{i}}+L_{i})=Y\cap\varphi^{-1}(\Theta_{i}).

  3. (3)

    Hence we have

    χ⁡(Y∩φ−1​(zi))=χ⁡(Y∩𝐕⁡(IWi+Li))deg⁡(Wi¯).\chi(Y\cap\varphi^{-1}(z_{i}))=\frac{\chi(Y\cap\mathbf{V}(I_{W_{i}}+L_{i}))}{\deg(\overline{W_{i}})}.

5.3. Feynman integrals

We conclude the paper with two examples of Feynman integrals from physics.

Example 5.11 (Bubble).

The example from the Introduction is on of the simplest Feynman integrals and we revisit this example here just to verify the result. We do this by again noting that this integral in fact fits within the GKZ framework. The hypergoemetric system HA​(β)H_{A}(\beta) annihilating this integral is generated by

and the support of this cycle is the same characteristic variety as obtained in the introduction.

This coincides with [18]. The rank of this DD-module is 8 and the characteristic cycle is

8​𝐂𝐨𝐧​(0)+2​𝐂𝐨𝐧​(p32−2)+𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(p32−1)+3​𝐂𝐨𝐧​(p32)+2​𝐂𝐨𝐧​(p32+1)+𝐂𝐨𝐧⁡(p32+2).8\mathbf{Con}(0)+2\mathbf{Con}(p_{3}^{2}-2)+\mathbf{Con}(p_{3}^{2}-1)+3\mathbf{Con}(p_{3}^{2})+2\mathbf{Con}(p_{3}^{2}+1)+\mathbf{Con}(p_{3}^{2}+2).

⋄\diamond
